title: Object permissions, field-level security, and record-level access
objectives: Name the three data-access layers: object permissions, field-level security, and record-level access.
Explain that profiles and permission sets grant object and field capability, while roles and sharing decide which records.
Diagnose 'cannot see Amount' as field-level security, not a missing share, when the record already opens.
Refuse to treat page layouts as field-level security.
diagnostic_question: LAB_Rep opens LAB_Opportunity_Orion but cannot see Amount and cannot edit Stage. Another user cannot find Orion at all. Which layer is each symptom, and what would you not change first?
definition: Salesforce data access has three gates. Object permissions (Create, Read, Update, Delete) are the bluntest control: they decide whether a user can act on any record of that type. Field-level security—field permissions—controls whether a user can see or edit a field's value, including in lists, reports, and search. Record-level access then decides which individual records a user can view or edit after those gates pass. ([Control Who Sees What](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_data_access.htm))
why_it_matters: A visibility ticket is often one sentence and three different layers. Fixing the wrong layer overexposes an object, hides a field for the wrong reason, or never opens the record. Interviewers listen for the order: object, then field, then record—and for the page-layout trap.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a hospital ward. Object permissions are whether your badge allows the cardiology ward at all. Field-level security is whether you may read the medication line on a chart. Record-level access is which patient rooms you may enter. A curtain on the chart holder (page layout) can hide a line on one screen without locking the field in reports. Sharing which rooms you enter is the next lesson; this one is the three gates.
deeper_explanation: Object-level security, or object permissions, is the bluntest way to control data access. You can prevent a user from seeing, creating, editing, or deleting any instance of an object type by using object permissions. You specify them in permission sets and profiles. ([Control Who Sees What](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_data_access.htm))

Field-level security, or field permissions, controls whether a user can see, edit, and delete the value for a particular field. Field permissions control visibility in related lists, list views, reports, and search results. To ensure a user cannot access a field, use field permissions. Page layouts only control visibility on detail and edit pages. ([Control Who Sees What](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_data_access.htm))

Record-level sharing settings, user roles, and sharing rules control the individual records users can view and edit. Permission sets and profiles control object and field access; roles primarily control record-level access. Sharing rules only widen access above organization-wide defaults; they cannot be stricter than OWD. The sharing stack itself is SEC-004. ([Control Who Sees What](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_data_access.htm))
A user needs both a permitted object or field action and a record-access path. A share cannot create missing Read on Opportunity or missing FLS on Amount.

mental_model.analogy: A hospital ward: badge-for-the-ward is object permissions, chart-line visibility is field-level security, which patient rooms you may enter is record-level access.
useful_mapping: medication line on the chart → field-level security
curtain on one clipboard → page layout (not FLS)
which rooms → record-level access (OWD, roles, sharing)
permission set / profile → who issues ward and chart rights
role → primarily which rooms, not the ward badge
where_it_breaks: View All / Modify All style object permissions can bypass the room-by-room model; treat those as Needs verification of exact names and impact in the org.
The hospital does not encode restriction rules (SEC-005) or Apex sharing keywords (SEC-006).

claims.claim: Object permissions are the bluntest data-access control and can prevent any create, read, edit, or delete of that object type. They are specified in permission sets and profiles.
claims.validation: Control Who Sees What, object-level security section.

claims.claim: Field permissions control field visibility in related lists, list views, reports, and search. Page layouts only control visibility on detail and edit pages.
claims.validation: Control Who Sees What, field-level security section.

claims.claim: Record-level sharing settings, roles, and sharing rules control which individual records a user can view or edit. Roles are not a substitute for object or field permissions.
Sharing rules give more access and cannot be stricter than organization-wide defaults.
claims.validation: Control Who Sees What sharing-rules paragraph.

changed_in_release: The three-layer model remains the Control Who Sees What teaching. Reverify permission-set vs profile UI in the target org.
unresolved_uncertainty: Exact names and impact of View All / Modify All style permissions should be confirmed in current Help for the target object.
Which standard objects support which sharing defaults is org- and edition-sensitive (SEC-004).

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: Object permissions decide if you can use the type. Field-level security decides if a field is visible or editable anywhere, not just on the layout. Record-level access decides which rows. A share cannot invent missing CRUD or FLS.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I diagnose in order. If the user cannot see any Opportunity, I check object Read. If they open Orion but miss Amount, I check field permissions and I do not trust a page-layout change. If they have Read and FLS but still miss Orion, I hand off to OWD, roles, and sharing. Profiles and permission sets own the first two gates; roles own the third primarily.

terminology.plain: Whether you can create, read, update, or delete that type of record at all.
terminology.precise: Object-level security specified in permission sets and profiles. The bluntest data-access control.
terminology.example: LAB_Rep has Opportunity Read and Update, not Delete.
terminology.non_example: A sharing rule granting one Opportunity is not an object permission.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: User permission: tasks and features such as View Setup.
terminology.boundary: View All / Modify All style grants are neighboring; confirm names in org Help.

terminology.plain: Whether a field's value is visible or editable for that user.
terminology.precise: Field permissions that apply in related lists, list views, reports, and search, not only on a page layout.
terminology.example: Amount hidden from LAB_Rep in reports as well as on the record page.
terminology.non_example: Removing Amount from a page layout while leaving FLS readable.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Page layout: detail and edit page presentation only.

terminology.plain: Which individual records you can open after object Read exists.
terminology.precise: Controlled by organization-wide defaults, roles, sharing rules, and related sharing mechanisms taught in SEC-004.
terminology.example: LAB_Rep has Opportunity Read but cannot open a peer-owned Private deal.
terminology.non_example: Missing Amount on a record they already opened.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Object Read: capability on the type, not a specific row.
terminology.boundary: This lesson names the layer; SEC-004 designs the stack.

terminology.plain: What fields appear on the detail and edit pages.
terminology.precise: Layouts control visibility on detail and edit pages only. They are not as protective as field permissions.
terminology.example: Amount off the LAB_Rep layout but still in a report if FLS allows.
terminology.non_example: Using a layout to 'secure' a salary field for all channels.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Dynamic Forms: presentation, still not FLS.
terminology.boundary: Lightning record pages are presentation (DATA/APP tracks).

terminology.plain: Create, Read, Update, Delete on an object.
terminology.precise: The object-permission actions that decide whether any instance of the type can be acted on.
terminology.example: Lead Delete granted in a permission set.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: User permission: org feature, not object CRUD.

terminology.plain: The FLS setting for one field.
terminology.precise: Controls seeing, editing, and deleting the field value across the app surfaces listed in Help.
terminology.example: Amount: readable, not editable for LAB_Rep.
terminology.non_example: A validation rule that blocks Stage changes.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Validation rule: data quality, not FLS.
terminology.boundary: Configured on permission sets and profiles.

when_to_use: When a ticket mixes object permissions, field-level security, and record-level access in one sentence.
When a user opens a record but a field is missing in reports as well as on the page.
When you must decide whether to grant object CRUD, change FLS, or leave the issue to sharing.
When someone claims a page layout is enough to secure a field.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this three-layer lesson to design the full OWD, role hierarchy, and sharing-rule stack (SEC-004).
Do not treat field-level security as Shield Platform Encryption (SEC-009).
Do not grant object-wide access to fix one missing record.
Do not use object permissions to solve an authentication or session failure (SEC-001).

Object Manager → field → field-level security (UI path can vary; reverify).
Sharing Settings only after the capability gates pass.
A report or list view to prove FLS beyond the page layout.

Stage edit is a separate object-Update plus field-edit question

decisions.rejected: Public Read/Write OWD so they can 'edit more'

Inspect Amount field permissions on LAB_Rep's permission set.
Inspect Opportunity Update and Stage FLS if edit is required.
For LAB_Peer, confirm Opportunity Read exists, then stop for SEC-004.

decision_table.signal: User cannot see any records of the type and tabs/search show nothing.

decision_table.why: Object permissions are the bluntest gate; a share cannot create missing Read.

decision_table.signal: User opens the record but a field is missing in the report too.
decision_table.why: Field permissions apply to reports, lists, and search; layouts do not.

decision_table.signal: User opens the record and sees the field but cannot edit it.

Using a sharing rule to hide a field.

interview_questions.question: Walk the three Salesforce data-access layers.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Object permissions are CRUD on the type. Field-level security is field visibility and edit across reports and search, not just the layout. Record-level access is which rows, via OWD, roles, and sharing.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I quote Control Who Sees What. Object permissions are the bluntest gate and live on permission sets and profiles. Field permissions protect more surfaces than a page layout. Record access is a separate stack I will design in the next topic. I always say a share cannot invent missing CRUD or FLS. That sentence is the interview closer.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep: Opportunity Read yes, Amount FLS hidden, Orion visible; LAB_Peer: Read yes, Orion not visible—record layer.
tradeoffs: Blunt object deny vs surgical FLS
Layout convenience vs real field protection
follow_ups: What cannot a sharing rule do to OWD?

interview_questions.question: Why are page layouts not field-level security?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Layouts only affect detail and edit pages. Field permissions also apply to lists, reports, and search. To keep a user from accessing a field, use FLS.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I treat layout work as UX. If a compliance stakeholder says 'take salary off the page,' I still inspect field permissions and run a report as that user. If the report shows the value, the field is not protected. I do not claim Dynamic Forms change that boundary unless current Help says so—I would mark that Needs verification.
interview_questions.example: Amount added back to the LAB_Rep layout still hidden in their report when FLS is off.
tradeoffs: Faster layout edit vs incomplete protection
Hiding UI clutter vs hiding data
weak_answer_warnings: Calling the layout a security control

interview_questions.question: User can open the Opportunity but cannot see Amount or edit Stage. Diagnose.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Record access already worked. I check Amount FLS and Opportunity Update plus Stage field-edit. I do not change OWD.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I reproduce as the user. Amount missing in a report means FLS, not layout. Stage visible but not editable means Update and/or field-edit. I compare a user who should edit Stage. I keep sharing out of the fix. If they had not found the record, I would have switched layers.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep on Orion: Amount FLS hidden; Stage read-only because field-edit is off while object Update is on.
tradeoffs: Granting object Update vs only field-edit
follow_ups: How would View All change this?
What if API still returns Amount?

interview_questions.question: A teammate wants Public Read/Write so a user can 'see the Amount field.' Response?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: OWD does not grant field permissions. If the record already opens, I fix FLS. If the record does not open, I still would not jump to Public Read/Write without a sharing design.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I separate the ask. Amount is a field. Public Read/Write is a record baseline that can expose every row. That violates least privilege and does not make a hidden field appear if FLS is off. I would demonstrate a report as the user. Then, if records are missing, I schedule the SEC-004 conversation instead of opening the object to the world.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep already opens Orion; Amount still hidden after a reckless OWD change because FLS never moved.
follow_ups: What is the correct sharing design if the record is missing?
How do you prove FLS independently?
weak_answer_warnings: Agreeing to Public Read/Write for a field issue

interview_questions.question: How do profiles, permission sets, and roles map onto the three layers?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Profiles and permission sets grant object and field capability. Roles primarily drive record-level access. I do not assign a role to grant Delete on Lead.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I keep SEC-002 in the answer: one profile, additive permission sets. Those stores hold CRUD and FLS. Roles sit on the record path with OWD and sharing rules. Interviewers bait a single 'access' word. I split capability versus row visibility. User permissions such as View Setup stay in a fourth bucket so I do not call them object permissions.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Analyst: Lead Delete in a permission set; East role only for hierarchy tests, not for Delete.
follow_ups: What is a permission-set group’s role here?

interview_questions.question: Field is missing on the page but present in a report. What is going on?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: FLS is allowing the field. The page layout or Lightning record page is not showing it. I do not tighten sharing.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I use the Help distinction as a diagnostic. Report visibility means field permissions are open. I inspect layout assignment, record type, and the Lightning page. I still ask whether the field should be in the report; if not, I close FLS rather than only the layout. I test as the intended user, not as admin.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep layout omits Amount; their LAB report still shows Amount until FLS is changed.

interview_questions.question: When do you stop this topic and start the sharing stack?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: When object CRUD and needed FLS are correct and the user still cannot reach a specific record. Then OWD, roles, and sharing rules own the work.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I write a one-line proof: 'capability yes, row no.' That sentence is the handoff. I will mention that sharing cannot tighten OWD, so if everyone already sees every row, a sharing rule will not hide one. Restriction rules are a later narrowing tool. I do not start Apex without sharing in this admin conversation.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Peer has Opportunity Read and Amount FLS; Orion still missing → SEC-004.
tradeoffs: Staying in capability vs jumping to sharing too early
View All as a blunt bypass vs a real sharing design
follow_ups: What if View All is already on?
weak_answer_warnings: Designing OWD inside the FLS answer

interview_questions.question: Teach the three layers with a hospital analogy, then break it.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Ward badge is object permissions, chart lines are FLS, rooms are records. It breaks for View All-style grants and for restriction rules that further hide rooms you could already enter.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I walk LAB_Rep through the ward. I show a curtain (layout) that does not hide the lab system (report). I show a room they cannot enter (record access) even with a ward badge. I then say Apex, encryption, and guest users are other buildings. I finish with least privilege: do not hand out a master ward key because one room was locked.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Rep has the Opportunity ward badge, Amount line hidden, Orion room open; LAB_Peer has the badge but not the Orion room.
tradeoffs: Memorable teaching vs precise Help nouns
Blunt object deny vs many FLS exceptions
follow_ups: Where does page layout sit in the hospital?
